data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive methodological rule grounded in verisimilitude and the logic of severe testing, not probability.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If verisimilitude cannot be formally defined without probabilistic measures (as per Tichý/Miller), this defense collapses.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the preference implicitly assumes the uniformity of nature to justify acting on past success, it smuggles in induction.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "Popper distinguishes between logical probability (which remains zero or undefined for universal laws) and corroboration (a report of past performance). The preference is rational because severe tests eliminate false theories, leaving those with higher potential truth-content (verisimilitude). Acting on the best-tested theory is the only rational strategy to approximate truth, even without a guarantee of success or an inductive inference that the future will resemble the past.", "premises": [], "schema": "deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1", "scope": {"covers": [], "excludes": []}, "simulation_refs": [], "uncertainties": []}
